paragraphs: The summer sun shone warm and sweet, without a cloud or hint of sleet. Up where the pines stand proud and high, beneath the bright blue Michigan sky, lay Houghton Lake, so calm and wide, with gentle ripples on the tide!

Aboard the peppy pontoon boat, the finest crew that was afloat: Dad Alex grinning at the wheel, with shiny hooks and rods of steel! Young Shane (age five, with eyes of blue), and brother Tyson, smiling too! Both buckled snug in safety vests, like orange robins in their nests!

And there sat Mom—Theresa dear, the patient fisher of the year! In cozy sweatshirt, warm and grey, she held her fishing rod all day. While little minnows danced in line, and bobbers drifted on the brine, Theresa hadn't had much luck—no perchy bite, no bass to pluck!

Shane tapped her knee and gave a wink, "Don't worry, Mom! Don't even blink! Let's say our special fishing cheer, to bring the hungry fishes near!" Shane, Tyson, Dad, and Mom began, the loudest chant in Michigan:
The engine rested by the weeds, among the swaying water-reeds. The water shimmered like a cup, when all at once—the line zipped up!

The slender yellow pole bent double toward a watery hole! The tip plunged down! The rod groaned low, like Robin Hood’s bent wooden bow! Theresa gasped and gripped it tight, her brown eyes sparkling with delight!

"I’ve got one!" cried the happy Mom, her quiet afternoon was gone! She spun the handle—CLICK-CRANK-SPIN! The unseen monster pulled her in! The reel shrieked out: ZRRRR-WHIRRR-SCREECH! Farther than any arm could reach!

"Oh my!" Mom gasped, "He's strong and stout! This isn't just a tiny trout! He pulls like five or six or eight! He must be twenty pounds of weight! It’s bigger than I've ever seen, the biggest fish there's ever been!"
Shane bounced in place with happy squeals, while Tyson laughed at spinning reels! They clapped their hands and stomped the floor, and shouted out the chant once more:

Theresa leaned across the seat, to pull the prize up to her feet. Crank-crank! She wound with all her might, her knuckles white, the line drawn tight! Her hooded sweatshirt hung down low, with two white drawstrings on the go!

And as she cranked with speedy zeal—WHOOOOOOP!—the strings caught in the reel! Snick-snack! The little handle twirled, and sucked the drawstrings in a whirl! The hoodie cords wrapped round and round, tightly against the spool-wheel bound!

Mom couldn’t pull! Mom couldn’t crank! She leaned towards the pontoon plank! "Oh help!" laughed Mom, surprised and stuck, "Look what became of my good luck! My sweatshirt’s hitched unto the line, and this big fish is doing fine!"

Dad Alex vaulted from the wheel, "Hold steady, Mom! I'll fix the reel!" Shane held the rod to keep it high, while Tyson watched with eagle eye! With gentle tugs and nimble hands, Dad loosened up the tangled strands! Zip! Snip! Pluck-pluck! The knots came free! And everyone yelled out with glee:
Now free to fight! Now free to pull! Theresa wound the spool up full! The water churned, the bubbles flew, up toward the pontoon and the crew!

Then—SWOOSH!—beside the silver side, broke through the surface, wild and wide, a creature grand, a creature bold, with scales of olive, green, and gold! A Northern Pike! So long and sleek, with duckbill snout and toothy cheek! At least two feet—a two-foot dread! Full twenty-four big inches spread!
"LOOK AT THAT PIKE!" Shane shouted high, his round blue eyes as wide as pie! "He's giant!" Tyson yelled in joy, "He's almost bigger than a boy!"

Theresa held him by the boat, the finest trophy all afloat! "Quick, Alex, grab the landing net!" cried Mom, "Before he gets upset!" Alex looked left, he looked around, he searched the bench, he searched the ground! He searched the box, he searched the deck, with hands on hips and craned-up neck!

Then Alex’s jaw dropped in surprise, with wide, comedic, startled eyes: "Oh NO!" cried Dad, "You won't believe! The net is on the dock, I grieve! We left the net back on the shore, beside the boathouse cabin door!"
Right as they stared in disbelief, the Northern Pike had sweet relief! He gave a wink, he gave a flip, he didn't want a boat ride trip!

The mighty pike rolled round and round, a somersault without a sound! He shook his head, he thrashed his tail, and whipped the lake just like a whale! POP! went the hook right out his jaw! The cleanest leap they ever saw! He splashed a shower of sparkling spray, and swished his tail and sped away!

Down through the lily pads he dived, the grandest pike that ever thrived! A tiny moment hung in air, with water dripping in their hair... Then Tyson giggled, Shane broke out, and Dad and Mom began to shout!

They looked at Mom's loose sweatshirt strings, and all the silly tangled things! "He got away!" cried Shane with glee, "A giant fish as big as me!" They slapped high-fives and hugged so tight, beneath the golden sunset light!

Sure, they were just a bit dismayed, the fish had won the game they played! But oh, the fun! The wild hullabaloo! The greatest catch they ever knew! And as the pontoon purred back home, across the pink and amber foam, they sang the chant for everyone, of Houghton Lake, the pike, and fun:
Goodnight, Shane. Goodnight, Tyson. Goodnight, Houghton Lake... and goodnight, big Northern Pike!
Shane hurried down the dock with his yellow fishing rod. His orange life jacket was buckled tight. “Do you think we’ll see a fish today?” he asked.
“Let’s find out,” said Dad. He helped Shane onto the pontoon and started the motor. The boat hummed across Houghton Lake. Near the shore, tall reeds swayed in the breeze.
Shane pointed to a quiet patch of water. “There. That looks like a good hiding place.” Dad cut the motor. The lake grew still. Shane leaned close and whispered their plan: “Watch the bobber.”
Dad helped Shane cast. The red and white bobber landed with a tiny plop. They watched it float between the reeds.
A leaf drifted past. “Is that a fish?” Shane asked. “Just a leaf,” said Dad. A turtle poked its nose above the water. “How about now?” “That’s our neighbor,” Dad whispered.
Then the bobber dipped. Once. Twice. Down it went! The rod bent in Shane’s hands. Dad put his hands beside Shane’s on the handle. “Ready?” he asked. Shane nodded. Together they reeled.
Something green burst out of the lake. Splash! Water sprinkled Shane’s cheeks. A bass shook its tail and dropped back beside the boat.
“It pulled back!” Shane laughed. “It sure did,” said Dad. They brought the fish close. Dad held it gently while Shane looked at its bright scales and wide mouth. “Hello, fish,” Shane said.
They let the bass slip back into the lake. For a moment it stayed near the boat. Then its tail flicked, and it vanished under the reeds.
On the ride home, Shane kept one hand on Dad’s arm and one on the yellow rod. “Can we come back?” he asked. “Of course,” said Dad. “Maybe we’ll see another one.”
Shane held his orange Roadrunner disc at the first tee. Far down the path stood a basket with silver chains. “I want to hear them ring,” he told Dad.
“Then let’s give it a try,” said Dad. He took his pink disc from the bag. Shane looked down the fairway. One big tree stood between him and the basket.
He pointed past the trunk. “Around the tree. Toward the chains.” Dad grinned. “That’s the plan.”
Shane stepped sideways and threw. The disc sailed past the big tree, then dropped into the pine needles. A squirrel on a branch gave a little chatter.
“It made it past the tree,” said Dad. Shane ran to his disc and tried again. This time it glided right toward the basket. For one breath, Shane thought it might go in. But it landed just short.
“So close,” he said. Dad nodded. “Now you’ve got an easy shot.” Shane picked up the Roadrunner and walked closer. He could see every link in the chains.
Shane held the disc with both hands. He took a breath, chose a spot in the middle of the chains, and tossed.
Ching! The disc dropped into the basket. Shane froze. Then he jumped so high Dad had to catch him.
“You heard it!” Dad said. “I made it ring!” Shane said. The squirrel chattered again, as if it had been waiting for that sound too.
Dad tapped his pink disc against Shane’s orange one. They walked to the next tee together. Shane carried the Roadrunner under his arm, already looking for the next basket.
Click went Shane’s helmet buckle. Dad checked the strap, then the brakes on Shane’s red and blue bike. “Ready?” he asked.
Shane rang his little silver bell. Ding! “Now I am.” They rolled down the path together. Dad rode close enough to talk, but Shane chose the way.
At the bend, Shane saw a puddle across the trail. He slowed down. “Can I go through it?” Dad checked that it was shallow. “You can. Keep your wheels straight.”
Shane aimed for the middle. The front wheel touched the water. Then the back wheel followed.
Splash! Cold drops flew onto his legs. Dad got a few drops too. Shane laughed and rang his bell. “Did you see that?” “Every bit of it,” said Dad.

Around the next turn stood the Big Hill. It looked much taller from the bottom. Shane stopped smiling for a moment. “That’s a lot of uphill,” he said. Dad stopped beside him. “We can go slowly. I’ll stay with you.”
Shane pedaled. The hill pushed back. He pedaled again. His legs felt tired, and the top still looked far away.
“One more push,” said Dad. Shane pushed. Then one more. Then one more. At last his front wheel rolled onto flat ground.
From the top, he could see the puddle shining below. It looked tiny now. “I did the whole hill,” he said, almost to himself.
Dad smiled. Shane rang his bell three times. Ding! Ding! Ding! They rested while the evening sky turned orange. Then they took the easy path home.
Snow covered the path, the trees, and the little bench at the bottom of the hill. Shane wore his red coat and pom-pom hat. Dad pulled their red sled by its rope.
“This hill looks bigger in snow,” Shane said. They climbed together. Halfway up, Shane stopped to catch his breath. Dad stopped too. “We have plenty of time,” he said.
At the top, Shane brushed snow from the sled. Dad sat behind him. Shane tucked his mittens around the sides. “Ready?” Dad asked. Shane gave a serious nod.
Dad gave the sled a push. Down they went.

The first bump made Shane bounce. “One!” The second made Dad’s hat slip over one eye. “Two!” On the third bump, the sled lifted for a tiny moment, then landed in soft snow. “Three!” they shouted together.
The sled slid into a drift and stopped. Snow flew over their boots. Shane lay back and looked at the white sky. Then he laughed so hard Dad started laughing too.
“Again?” Shane asked. Dad looked up at the long hill. “After we warm up.”
They made snow angels beside the sled. Shane’s angel had small wings. Dad’s was so big that one wing touched the path.
On the bench, Dad opened a thermos of cocoa. Shane held his cup with both mittens. A marshmallow floated on top. After one sip, a white smudge sat above his lip.
Dad pointed to his own mouth. Shane wiped the wrong side of his face. Dad laughed and helped him find it.
The hill was quiet now. They watched the last sledders head home. “We can ride again tomorrow,” Dad said. Shane leaned against him and took one more warm sip.
Shane sat on the rug in his pajamas. Dad shuffled the Uno cards beside the fire. “One game before bed,” Dad said.
Shane looked at his hand. Red, blue, yellow, green—and one card he tucked behind the others. Dad laid down a blue card. Shane matched it. Dad played another. Back and forth the colors went.
Shane kept peeking at his hidden card. Dad noticed. “Do you have a plan?” he asked. “Maybe,” said Shane. He tried not to smile.
Shane played a red card. Now he held just one. “UNO!” he called.
Dad sat up. “Only one? Then I’d better think.” He chose a green card and set it on the pile. Shane looked at the green card. Then he looked at his own. Dad leaned forward.
“Can you play?” Dad asked. Shane waited one long second. “Yes,” he said. He turned over his last card: Wild Draw Four!
Dad stared at the card. “You saved that the whole time?” Shane nodded. Dad drew four cards, counting them aloud. “One, two, three, four.”
“I won!” Shane said. Dad gave him a high five. “You did. And you were very sneaky.”
They put the cards back in the box. The fire crackled. Shane curled up beside Dad for a moment before bed.
“Same time tomorrow?” Shane asked. “Deal,” said Dad. “But tomorrow I’m watching that secret card.”
Shane carried his orange Roadrunner disc into Whispering Woods. Dad carried a pink one. Sunlight made bright spots on the path.
“First one to hear the chains?” Dad asked. Shane nodded and hurried to the tee. He liked the sound a disc made when it landed in the basket: ching!
Shane stood sideways and threw. His disc sailed over the grass and landed in the middle of the fairway. Dad gave him a high five. Dad’s pink disc landed near the basket.
Shane made a short toss. Ching! The chains rattled. “That’s my favorite sound,” he said. They picked up their discs and went deeper into the woods.
At the next tee, the path narrowed between tall trees. Shane threw hard. A gust of wind caught the Roadrunner and tipped it into the ferns.
Plip. Then silence.
Shane searched under one leaf, then another. No orange disc. Dad took his hand. “We’ll look together.” A faint ting came from farther in. They followed the sound past a mossy tree.
In a clearing stood a basket wrapped in purple flowers. Beside it were a white squirrel, a small hedgehog, and a spotted baby deer. Shane’s Roadrunner lay between them.
“There it is!” Shane whispered. The squirrel lifted one edge. The hedgehog pushed from behind. The deer gave the disc a final nudge with its nose. Up it popped—and down into the basket. Ching!
Shane laughed. “You made it ring!” He picked up his disc and thanked each animal. The squirrel chirped. The deer dipped its head.

Dad tapped his pink disc against the orange one. The animals slipped back into the ferns, leaving the basket quiet again. Shane and Dad walked on. Every few steps, Shane looked over his shoulder, hoping to hear one more little ting.
At hole ten, Shane’s orange Roadrunner landed beside a pile of leaves. As he reached for it, he spotted a feather almost as long as his arm.
“Who dropped this?” he asked. Dad turned it over. Brown and black stripes ran across it. “A big bird,” Dad said. Shane slipped the feather into his bag. “Then we have a mystery.”
They followed the path to a creek. In the soft mud were three-toed prints. Some were big. Some were tiny.
“Dinosaur feet?” Shane whispered. Dad crouched beside him. “Maybe bird feet. Look at the little ones.” Shane imagined a big bird walking with its babies. “Let’s see where they went.”
At hole twelve, Shane threw past a fallen log. Before he could fetch his disc, something scratched in the leaves.
Scratch, scratch. Cluck.
Shane held Dad’s hand. They moved quietly to the log and peeked over. Something brown and round moved in a patch of sunlight. Then four smaller shapes hurried after it.
It was a family of wild turkeys. One big turkey spread its tail like a fan. Another scratched the ground. Four fluffy chicks followed close behind.
One chick pecked the edge of Shane’s orange disc. Tock, tock. Shane covered his mouth so he would not laugh too loudly.
The big turkey called, “Gobble, gobble!” The chicks hurried away with their parents. Shane waited until they were gone before picking up his disc.
Shane held up the feather. Its stripes matched the big turkey’s tail. He looked back at the three-toed tracks. “It was them!” he said.

Dad tapped his pink disc against Shane’s Roadrunner. “Good looking, detective.” Shane put the feather safely in his bag. They walked to the next hole, watching the leaves in case another clue appeared.
Shane and Dad reached Miller’s Creek just as the sun came up. Shane wore his orange life jacket and carried his yellow fishing rod. Dad carried the tackle box.
“Do you think Big Walter is awake?” Shane asked. Dad had told him about the old catfish in the creek. “Maybe,” Dad said. “Let’s ask him.” They sat together on the dock and cast into the quiet water.
A turtle rested on a log. Dragonflies darted over the creek. Shane’s red and white bobber barely moved.

Then it vanished. The yellow rod bent toward the water. “Dad!” Shane cried. Dad moved beside him and held the rod too. “I’ve got you,” he said. They pulled together, one slow turn of the reel at a time.
A wide gray head rose from the water. Long whiskers spread out from its mouth. Shane stared. “That’s Big Walter!”
The catfish gave one heavy swish of its tail. Dad kept the line steady while Shane reeled. At last they guided Walter into the shallows beside the dock.
“He’s bigger than my backpack,” Shane said. Dad laughed. “A lot bigger.”
Dad laid Walter for a moment on the damp grass beside the creek and kept a hand on him. Shane leaned in. The catfish was smooth and gray, with long whiskers by his mouth.
“Can I take a picture?” Shane asked. Dad handed him the phone. Shane took one quick photo.
“What should we do now?” Dad asked. Shane looked at the creek. “Let him go home,” he said. Together they slid Walter back into the water.
For a moment Walter stayed beside them. Then he flicked his tail. Splash! Cold creek water spotted Shane’s life jacket and Dad’s shirt.
They laughed as the big shape disappeared below the dock. Shane waved at the water. “Bye, Walter.”
On the walk home, Shane carried the yellow rod. Dad carried the tackle box. Both of them were still a little wet, and both knew exactly what story they would tell at breakfast.
The moon was a crescent, the stars were in sight,And Mt. Pleasant was settling into the night.
Young Shane brushed his teeth till they sparkled like snow,Then hopped in his bed with a five-year-old glow.
His blankets were pulled to his chin, warm and neat,Tucked snug from his ears right on down to his feet.
In walked his mom, Theresa, smiling and kind,With glasses in place and a story in mind.
She sat on the mattress and opened the book,And gave little Shane her sweet motherly look.
She opened her mouth for the very first word,When suddenly—TOOT!—came the weirdest sound heard.
A squeak like a mouse on a tiny brass horn!The funniest noise since the day Shane was born.
Shane opened his eyes and he poked out his head:“Did someone just blow a kazoo near my bed?”
Theresa turned pink. “Oh, dear me, that was odd!“A squeak in the floorboards!” she claimed with a nod.
She cleared out her throat and she straightened her spine,“Now back to our tale of the brave porcupine...”
She leaned just an inch to turn over page three,When out slipped a rumble as loud as the sea!
PBBBBBT-whistle-POP! went the seat of the chair,A gust that tossed ribbons of dust in the air.
Shane burst out laughing. “Mom, that wasn’t the floor!“That sounded like thunder behind the front door!”
Theresa pressed tight on her lips with a blush,“Hush, sweetheart,” she whispered, “now listen and hush!”
She pinched her knees shut and she held in her breath;She tried to stay quieter than silent death.
She squeezed and she squirmed and she counted to eight,Her tummy was rumbling like heavy freight.
“I’m fine,” Theresa said, “it’s just broccoli from lunch,“Or maybe the fiber bar snacks that I munch!”
She stood up to pat Shane’s soft pillow in place,Determined to salvage a straight, solemn face.
She bent at the waist, gave the pillow a fluff—And HONK! went her belly! A giant steam puff!
TOOT-A-LOO! BUBBLE-POP! PARP-ITY-WHEEZE!The window blinds rattled from Mom’s little breeze!
Now Shane lost his marbles; he rolled on the sheets,His giggles as sweet as the baker’s best treats.
He kicked up his heels and he clutched at his vest:“Mom, you’re an orchestra! You are the best!”
Theresa looked down, and she started to grin;There wasn’t a chance she could hold it all in.
She chuckled, she snorted, and out came three more:Pip-pop! and a bop! as she stepped toward the door!
“Well, Shane,” chuckled Mom, wiping tears from her eyes,“I didn’t intend for bedtime surprise!
It seems that my motor just won’t settle down,I might just toot-toot all the way across town!”
Shane sat right up and he gave her a hug,Wrapped safe in his blankets so cozy and snug.
“Don’t worry, sweet Mom, it’s the best book by far—“You toot like a rocket that shoots for a star!”
Theresa smoothed back Shane’s neat spiky brown hair,And gave him a kiss on his cheek right then there.
“Goodnight, little buddy. Sweet dreams until dawn.”She gave a big stretch and a sleepy, slow yawn.
She switched off the lamp with a gentle soft click,And tiptoed outside on her toes very quick.
And just as the door closed, as quiet could be...One final soft toot floated out full of glee.
Tyson and his dad, Alex, went to the lake. Tyson had his rod. Dad had the worms. Both had their life jackets on.
“I will catch a big fish!” said Tyson. Dad put a worm on the hook. Tyson cast his line. Plop! His red float sat on the water.
They sat. They waited. A duck swam past. “Do you know where the fish are?” Tyson asked it. “Quack,” said the duck. “That was not much help,” said Dad.
Then the float went down. “Dad! I have one!” Tyson held his rod up. He turned the reel. The line pulled hard. “It must be huge!” he said.
Dad got the net. Tyson reeled some more. Up came a stick.
Tyson stared at it. Dad stared at it. “That fish has a lot of legs,” said Dad.
Tyson laughed so hard his hat fell off. Dad caught it in the net. “One stick and one hat!” said Tyson.
He tried again. This time, he cast near some weeds. Plop. Wait. Tug! A small fish flashed in the sun. Dad helped bring it in.
“My first real fish!” said Tyson. It was no bigger than his hand. Dad took a photo. Then they let the fish go. Splash! Water hit Dad right on the nose.
Tyson grinned. “Small fish. Big splash!” On the way home, Dad asked, “What was your best catch?” “The fish,” said Tyson. “But you caught a pretty nice hat.”
Tyson and his mom, Theresa, were at the park. A yellow tail poked out of a bush. “Pika?” Tyson bent down. It was Pikachu!
“Hi!” said Tyson. “What is wrong?” Pikachu pointed up. A red ball sat in a tree. “Your ball is stuck,” said Mom.
Tyson looked at the low branch. He could not reach it. “I have a plan,” he said. “Can we shake the tree?” Mom held the trunk. Tyson held it, too. They gave it a small shake.
One leaf fell. It landed on Pikachu’s head. “Nice hat,” said Tyson.
Pikachu shook off the leaf. The ball did not move. Tyson sat on the grass to think. Then he saw a long blue tube in Mom’s bag. His pool noodle!
“Can we use that?” he asked. Mom held up the soft noodle. It just reached the ball. Tap. Tap. Nothing. “Try from this side,” said Tyson. Mom moved. Tyson stood back with Pikachu. Tap!
The ball fell. Boing! It hit the grass. Boing! It bounced right into Mom’s open bag. Pikachu ran to the bag. Out came the ball. Out came a sock, too. Pikachu had the sock on one ear!

Tyson giggled. “That is an even better hat.” They played catch on the grass. Tyson threw. Mom caught. Pikachu rolled the ball back. At last, it was time to go. Pikachu gave Tyson a soft hug. “Same park next time?” asked Tyson. “Pika, pika!” Tyson smiled. He was sure that meant yes.
Tyson was seven, and he loved flag football. Today, his dad, Alex, came to watch. Tyson had two blue flags on his belt. He tucked in his shirt. He was ready.
On his first run, he went left. A kid pulled his flag. On his next run, he went right. A kid pulled his flag again. Tyson sat by Dad for a drink. “They get me every time,” he said.

Dad took a sip, too. “What do you see when you run?” “The kid in front of me.” “What else could you look for?” Tyson looked at the field. He saw kids. He saw flags. Then he saw a wide patch of open grass. “A space!” he said.

Back in the game, Tyson got the ball. He looked up. A kid ran toward him. Tyson took one step left. The kid went left, too. Then Tyson cut right. There was the space! Run, run, run! His flags flapped behind him. He crossed the line. His team cheered. Dad jumped up. His hat fell into his lap.
On the next play, Tyson’s friend Ben fell. The ball rolled away. Tyson stopped and held out his hand. Ben got up. “Thanks,” said Ben. Soon, Ben made a great catch. Tyson cheered the loudest.
After the game, Dad gave Tyson a high five. “Did you see my run?” asked Tyson. “I sure did. I saw you help Ben, too.” Tyson grinned. “Next time, hold on to your hat!”
Tyson and his mom, Theresa, found a green pipe. A red cap popped out. “Mario!” said Tyson. Mario climbed up. “I need help. My star is gone!” “We can look,” said Mom.
They went down the pipe. Whoosh! They landed on soft grass. There were big blocks in the sky. “Where did you see it last?” asked Tyson. “By that hill,” said Mario.
They went up the hill. Something yellow shone by a rock. “My star!” said Mario. But it was a banana peel. “Good thing we did not step on it,” said Mom. They put it in a bin.
Then Tyson heard a sound. Sniff. Sniff. Yoshi sat by a bush. He had a tear on his cheek. “What is wrong?” asked Tyson. Yoshi pointed to his foot. A small thorn was stuck in it.
Mom took out the thorn with care. Tyson held Yoshi’s hand. “All done,” said Mom.

Yoshi stood up. He gave a happy hop. Ding! A bright star fell from the bush. “There it is!” said Mario. Yoshi had been sitting right next to it. Tyson picked up the star. It felt warm in his hands. He gave it to Mario.

“You found my star!” said Mario. “And we found someone who needed help,” said Mom. Mario led them back to the pipe. Yoshi waved. Whoosh! They were home. Tyson looked at his shoes. One had a big green spot. “Grass from Mario’s world!” he said. Mom smiled. “Let’s keep that part off the couch.”
Tyson and his dad, Alex, put on their helmets. They rode their bikes on the park path. Ding, ding! Tyson rang his bell.
Up ahead, a boy stood by a bench. He was looking under it. “Did you lose something?” asked Tyson.
“My toy car,” said the boy. “It is red. It was in my pocket.” Tyson and Dad stopped their bikes. They got off to help. “Where did you go?” asked Tyson. “To the swings. Then here.”
They looked by the swings. No car. They looked by the slide. No car. Dad found a red leaf. “Does your car have a stem?” he asked. The boy gave a small smile. “No.”
Tyson looked down the path. There was a hill between the swings and the bench. “Cars roll,” he said. “Maybe it went down there.” They walked to the foot of the hill.
Tyson saw a red dot in the grass. He bent down. A bottle cap. “Not yet,” he said. Then he saw four tiny wheels. They stuck up from behind a pine cone. “Found it!”
The boy hugged his car. “Thanks!” He rolled it on the bench. It went fast. “Your car had a big trip,” said Tyson. Tyson and Dad got back on their bikes. “You used a good clue,” said Dad.
Tyson rang his bell. Ding, ding! “What is that for?” asked Dad. “It means the car finder is back at work!” Just then, Dad dropped his glove. Tyson laughed. “Another job!”
Tyson and his mom, Theresa, went to the pond. They wore life jackets and sat on the dock. Tyson cast his line. Plop!
A round head popped up. “Squirtle!” said Tyson. The little Pokémon waved. “Do you like to fish?” asked Mom. Squirtle nodded. Then it ducked under the water.
Tyson’s float bobbed. Once. Twice. He lifted his rod. At the end of the line was a wet leaf. Squirtle popped up and clapped. “That is not a fish!” said Tyson.

Squirtle looked at the leaf. Then it looked at Tyson. It gave a big grin. Tyson cast again. Plop! The float bobbed. Tyson reeled in. This time, he had a small twig. Squirtle clapped even harder. “Are you putting things on my hook?” asked Tyson. Squirtle hid its face. But Tyson could see its grin.
Mom laughed. “I think we have a pond prank.” Tyson set his rod down. “I have a new game,” he said. Mom put a leaf on the water. It was shaped like a boat. “Can you push it to that reed?”
Squirtle blew a tiny puff of water. The leaf spun in a circle. “Too much!” said Tyson. Squirtle tried a soft puff. The leaf slid to the reed. “You did it!”
Then Squirtle gave one happy splash. Plop! A drop landed on Tyson’s nose. Mom held out a towel. “Did we catch any fish?” she asked. “No,” said Tyson. “But we found a very silly friend.”
Tyson brushed and stopped to stare; A tiny tooth was wobbling there. “My first loose tooth!” he cried with glee. “A wiggly tooth belongs to me!”
Dad, Alex, said, “Let's see it go— Just gentle wiggles, nice and slow.” Theresa smiled, her eyes so bright: “We'll let it go when time is right.”
With clean hands, Tyson gently tried; That little tooth went side to side. He nudged it with his tongue once more; It held on tighter than before.
“Wiggle, wobble! Won't you fall?” It would not budge much more at all. “Let's take a break,” he heard Dad say. So Tyson dashed outside to play.
The trampoline was round and green, The bounciest thing he'd ever seen. Its net zipped shut; Mom watched nearby, While Tyson bounced beneath the sky.
A little hop! A happy spin! A breeze tickled his cheek and chin. He laughed and bounced above the ground; His tooth slipped out without a sound.
It tumbled past the padded side And in the grass it went to hide. No tiny tap. No shout of “Hey!” He never felt it slip away.
When play was done, he touched his chin. His tongue explored his toothy grin. He found a gap! His eyes grew round: “My tooth is gone—but can't be found!”
They searched the grass; they checked each shoe. They looked beneath the trampoline, too. But not a speck of tooth was there. Tyson sniffled in the evening air.
“No tooth beneath my pillow tonight! The fairy won't come on her flight!” Mom hugged him close. Dad held him tight. “Let's leave a note,” said Mom. “We'll write.”
Dear Tooth Fairy, my tooth came free While I was bouncing happily. I didn't notice it fall that day; It landed somewhere far away.
We searched and searched, but couldn't see The little tooth that came from me. Please visit even though it's gone. Love, Tyson. Then he gave a yawn.
He tucked the note, then climbed in bed. Mom kissed his cheek; Dad stroked his head. The moon shone softly, silver-white; His little room grew still that night.
On whisper-wings, a fairy flew And read the note that told her true. “A missing tooth? That's quite all right. Your note has brought me here tonight.”
She left a dollar, crisp and green, Beneath his pillow, quite unseen. At dawn he peeked—then gave a shout: “She came! She came! It all worked out!”
Theresa laughed; Dad grinned along. His tooth was lost, but hope stayed strong. One dollar! One new gap to show! And one more way for him to grow.

But this was too much. The wolf danced about with rage and swore he would come down the chimney and eat up the little pig for his supper. But while he was climbing on to the roof the little pig made up a blazing fire and put on a big pot full of water to boil. Then, just as the wolf was coming down the chimney, the little piggy pulled off the lid, and plop! in fell the wolf into the scalding water.
